arguments.heading: Argument analysis: March 24, 2026 session
paragraphs: This was the only argument session in the approved record. Gregory G. Garre appeared for the challenger. Frederick Liu appeared for the United States as a friend of the court supporting vacatur. William M. Jay appeared for Buddy Ayers Construction.

The challenger asked the Court to vacate and remand, limiting its argument to bankruptcy. Its reasoning centered on intent to adopt inconsistent positions, honest mistakes, and the debtor's own intent rather than the lawyer's.
The United States asked the Court to vacate and remand. Its reasoning was that the Fifth Circuit narrowed inadvertence and ignored a broader equitable balance.
Buddy Ayers asked the Court to affirm the lower result. Its reasoning was that mutuality is not required, the doctrine protects court integrity, and finality outweighs avoiding a windfall.

The justices tested assumptions about presumptions of intent, the role of the bankruptcy court, windfalls, client responsibility for lawyers, and whether state or federal law governs. No reargument occurred, so nothing was revisited on that basis.

case.dek: A Supreme Court case about when a bankruptcy debtor can be stopped from taking opposite positions in different cases.

dek_sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case involves a doctrine called judicial estoppel. It stops a person from taking one position in one case and the opposite position in another. The dispute here comes out of a bankruptcy case. The question is when that doctrine should apply to a debtor who left something off a bankruptcy form.

The doctrine matters because courts want honest answers in legal proceedings. If someone says one thing to one court and the opposite to another, courts worry about being misled. That is the integrity idea behind it.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Fifth Circuit, a federal appeals court, decided this dispute first. According to the challenger, that court applies a conclusive presumption of intent when a debtor knows about an asset and has a motive to hide it. The challenger says that presumption is too strict.

The United States, appearing as a friend of the court, describes the lower ruling differently. It says the Fifth Circuit narrowed the idea of an honest mistake and ignored a broader balancing of fairness factors. The Supreme Court heard oral argument on March 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The challenger asks the Court to vacate the lower ruling and send the case back for a fresh look. The United States takes the same requested result: vacate and remand. The other side, Buddy Ayers Construction, asks the Court to leave the lower ruling in place and keep the estoppel doctrine as it currently operates.
The challenger also narrowed its own ask during argument. It said its argument is confined to the bankruptcy context. It also conceded that the bankruptcy case can be reopened.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The challenger argues that intent to adopt inconsistent positions is the key thing. It says misleading the court is the heartland of the doctrine, and other factors may be considered. It also says intent to mislead is not strictly required, in its view.

The challenger adds that there should be no strong presumption of intent here. It points to confusing forms and many unsophisticated debtors. It says the bankruptcy court's own role and actions should count as an important factor. It also says there is no practical difference between knowing and intentional inconsistency.

Buddy Ayers answers that mutuality is not required. The doctrine protects court integrity, and it is unusual to have the same parties in a second case. It rejects the concern about integrity and accessibility, comparing the doctrine to rules that bind nonparties in some situations.

Buddy Ayers also says the system prioritizes finality and integrity over avoiding a windfall. It identifies the debtor's advantage as confirmation of a Chapter 13 plan, with an initial trustee objection about creditor treatment.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: The justices pressed both sides on how intent should be figured out. Justice Alito asked whether a duty to disclose plus a financial interest should create a presumption of intent. Justice Jackson asked how to treat an intentional omission that was not aimed at misleading the court.

Justice Thomas asked whether evidence matters to a holistic analysis, and what distinguishes Buddy Ayers' rule from the Fifth Circuit's rule. Chief Justice Roberts asked whether judicial integrity is the primary basis for the doctrine. Justice Barrett raised an Erie concern, which here means whether state or federal law governs the doctrine in cases between parties from different states.

Justice Kagan asked about how the Court has treated honest mistakes, referencing a government footnote. Justice Gorsuch asked how a windfall affects judicial integrity and accessibility. Justice Barrett also asked about the bankruptcy court's role in policing omissions and the timing of an amended schedule. Justice Alito asked about knowledge requirements and whether a client answers for a lawyer's omission.
Justice Thomas asked how the challenger responds to the claimed windfall for Buddy Ayers. Justice Jackson asked what advantage the debtor actually gained here.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The challenger lists factors courts could weigh: debtor testimony, sophistication, timing, notice to counsel, creditor objections, creditor impact, and bankruptcy findings. It says honest mistakes should generally preclude estoppel, and it accepts a narrow vacatur.

The challenger also says the record is silent on the attorney's omission, the debtor told the attorney, and the focus should stay on the debtor's own intent. A client is not ordinarily responsible in the same way for a lawyer's mistake.

Buddy Ayers counters that finality and court integrity justify the current approach. The United States supports a narrower path: vacate and remand so the lower court can apply a broader equitable balance.
